Methods

Data

This study uses Patient-Generated Health Data (PGHD) from the VA Wearable Technology Program, in which Veterans voluntarily enrolled and shared wearable device data (Fitbit, Garmin, or Apple Health). Data were obtained from January 01, 2022 through April 14, 2026. Daily step counts from Fitbit and Garmin devices were prioritized (using the higher value when both were present); Apple Health data served as an alternative when Fitbit/Garmin data were unavailable. A total of 8,858,283 patient-days had usable step data; Fitbit/Garmin data were available for 13.3% and Apple Health for the remainder. Daily step counts of zero were treated as missing, and outliers were removed using the 1.5×IQR method applied to raw device columns. Where step data were missing but exercise duration (minutes) was recorded, steps were imputed from a linear regression model fit on matched days (steps ~ exercise_minutes).

Cohort Derivation (Figure 1)

The analytic cohort was drawn from Veterans who had enrolled in the VA Wearable Technology Program with PGHD data available from January 01, 2022 through April 14, 2026. The single eligibility criterion was a first PGHD upload on or before March 16, 2025 (N = 13,184), derived as the latest first-upload date for which 52 weeks of potential observation remain before the data extract end date. This ensures a uniform 52-week observation window for every included patient. We then applied a weekly data quality filter requiring at least four upload days per 7-day window (miss_days ≤ 3), and retained only patients who had at least one qualifying week in the baseline period (calendar weeks 1–6; days 1–42 after each patient’s actual first upload date) and at least one qualifying observation week (week 7 onward). Calendar weeks are indexed relative to each patient’s actual first upload date (week 1 = days 1–7, week 2 = days 8–14, etc.). Patients whose composite event (ED visit, inpatient admission, or death) occurred within the first 42 days after first upload (calendar weeks 1–6) were additionally excluded, as no event-free anchor period exists for them. Observation windows were then censored at the date of a first composite event or at 52 weeks from first upload, whichever came first. The final analytic cohort included 10,112 Veterans contributing 322,774 person-weeks of observation (weeks 7+).

Step Feature Construction

At each observation week, a suite of step-derived features was computed from the 7-day, 14-day, and 21-day rolling windows anchored to the calendar week end-date. The primary current-activity features include the 7-day rolling average daily step count (k_steps_7d_avg, thousands), the rolling standard deviation (k_steps_7d_sd), the number of missing days in the window (k_steps_7d_miss_days), and the count of days with <1,000 steps (low_activity_days_7d). Two change metrics capture temporal trends: percent change from the average of the prior three 7-day windows (k_steps_7d_avg_pctdiff, winsorized at ±500%) and percent change from the 6-week baseline average (k_steps_7d_pct_from_baseline). Analogous 14-day and 21-day rolling averages and standard deviations provide longer-horizon smoothed signals. Two baseline summary features — mean steps and mean missing days across weeks 1–6 — anchor the within-person normalization.

Taken together, the step features implement a Mundlak-style decomposition for the primary activity signal. baseline_k_steps_avg — the patient’s mean daily step count across the six baseline weeks, fixed at enrollment — serves as the between-person anchor, capturing stable individual-level activity capacity. k_steps_7d_pct_from_baseline and k_steps_7d_avg_pctdiff represent within-person deviations from that anchor, capturing departures from the patient’s own history over medium and short horizons respectively. Because the baseline is computed exclusively from pre-observation data (weeks 1–6), all deviation features are computable at any future prediction point without requiring knowledge of future step counts — a prerequisite for prospective deployment.

Outcome Definition

The primary outcome was a composite of ED visit, inpatient admission, or death occurring within the prediction horizon (14 or 30 days) following a given observation week’s end date. The outcome was labeled positive (Y = 1) if any component occurred within 1 to h days (days_to_event ∈ [1, h]), and negative (Y = 0) otherwise. Observations within 30 days of the end of follow-up without a recorded event were excluded if the outcome window was not fully observed.

Statistical Analysis

We fit three feature sets: (1) step-derived features only (baseline + dynamic, n = 14 features); (2) static clinical features only (demographics, comorbidity flags, prior healthcare utilization, vitals, labs, and social history); and (3) the combined set. For each feature set and each prediction horizon (14-day and 30-day), we trained two algorithm types: penalized logistic regression (with elastic-net preprocessing) and gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost). Patients were randomly assigned to training (70%) and testing (30%) sets; all observation-weeks for a given patient remained in the same partition. To address class imbalance, logistic regression models were trained on patient-aware 3:1 undersampled data with case weights applied proportionally; XGBoost models were trained on the full (non-undersampled) training data with scale_pos_weight set to the true negative-to-positive ratio, avoiding the probability compression that results from training and scoring on different class distributions. Predicted probabilities were Platt-scaled (logistic calibration) on the test set; Platt-scaled probabilities were used to compute AUC-ROC and PR-AUC. Calibration slope was computed on the raw (pre-calibration) model output to provide an unbiased measure of model calibration. Brier score was computed but is not reported as a primary metric, as the low event rate (<3% per week) renders it statistically equivalent to the null (intercept-only) model.
